props.title: Mannequin

sections.content: Mannequin perfectly captures the quirky romantic comedy excess of the 1980s, following department store window dresser Jonathan Switcher (Andrew McCarthy) who falls in love with a mannequin possessed by an ancient Egyptian spirit (Kim Cattrall). The film shares DNA with other fantasy-romance hits of the era like Splash (1984) and Big (1988), riding the wave of magical realism that dominated mainstream comedy. While critically panned, it became a surprise box office success and cultural touchstone, particularly thanks to its infectious theme song "Nothing's Gonna Stop Us Now" by Starship and the scene-stealing performance of Meshach Taylor as flamboyant window dresser Hollywood Montrose.

sections.content: The film reflects the materialism and consumer culture of the 1980s through its department store setting. Like Working Girl (1988) and Nine to Five (1980), it uses corporate America as both backdrop and antagonist. The Prince & Company department store becomes a character itself, representing old money Philadelphia struggling against modernization. The elaborate window displays created by Jonathan and Emmy mirror the excess and theatrical presentation of 1980s culture, while also nodding to classic Hollywood musicals through their elaborate staging.

While often dismissed as pure camp, Mannequin explores themes of artistic expression and authenticity that resurface in later films like 500 Days of Summer (2009) and Ruby Sparks (2012). Jonathan's relationship with Emmy allows him to embrace his creative passion for window dressing, challenging traditional masculinity in ways that were progressive for 1987. The film's use of Egyptian mythology and reincarnation also connects it to supernatural romances like Ghost (1990) and Prelude to a Kiss (1992). SUBHEAD: Legacy and Cultural Impact

sections.content: The success of Mannequin spawned a sequel, Mannequin Two: On the Move (1991), and influenced a wave of inanimate object romance films like Life-Size (2000). Its blend of fantasy, romance, and workplace comedy created a template followed by films like Night at the Museum (2006). The film's exploration of art and commerce through window dressing presages later retail-set films like Mr. Magorium's Wonder Emporium (2007) and Confessions of a Shopaholic (2009).
